title: Nurse-led titration clinic for heart failure medicines in a district general hospital
subtitle: Service decision with a monitoring plan; no study family chosen yet
statement: Most of the 540 patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction followed by the service are below the target doses of guideline medicines: in the six months to June, 61 of 214 patients seen were on at least half the target dose of every medicine they could take. Titration happens at cardiology appointments every four to six months, so optimisation takes a year or more. The service has to decide whether to set up a nurse-led titration clinic run by its two nurse prescribers as a routine service or to study it first, and what to monitor once it runs.
whoAffected: Adults with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction under the hospital's heart failure service, especially those recently discharged, older patients and patients living far from the hospital; the two nurse prescribers; the cardiologists whose clinics carry the titration work now.
whatHurts: Patients spend months on starting doses of medicines that reduce admissions and deaths at target doses, and some are readmitted before the next cardiology appointment. Doses change rarely because each change waits for a consultant slot.
currentPractice: Dose changes at cardiology clinic every four to six months; the specialist nurses see patients for symptoms and education but do not titrate; blood tests are arranged ad hoc.
whyNow: A June clinic check showed 61 of 214 patients at half target dose or more, the nurses are ready to prescribe, the cardiology lead has signed off a draft protocol, and SGLT2 inhibitors have added a fourth class to titrate.
constraints: No research funding. The two nurse prescribers can give up to 6 clinic hours per week between them. Any new clinic must fit the existing heart failure service staffing and the trust's non-medical prescribing policy.
patientCenteredGoal: Patients reach the best doses they can tolerate within months rather than a year, with few blood tests and visits that fit their lives, and without harm from high potassium, low blood pressure or kidney injury.
summary: Problem framed as a service decision about a nurse-led titration clinic; no study design is assumed.
